messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Product Manager
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Rajesh

Rajesh was forty-two when armed men arrived at his apartment in Karachi. He had been a consultant then, advising on infrastructure projects for international firms—work that kept him moving between South Asia and the Gulf. That evening, three uniformed officers forced their way inside. What followed was three days of interrogation in a basement cell: repeated beatings, water poured over his face until he gasped for air, questions shouted in Urdu and English that blurred together into incomprehensible noise. They wanted information about his clients, his contacts, his movements. He had nothing to give them. By the third day, Rajesh no longer knew if he was being asked anything at all or if the voices were simply echoing in his own mind. When they finally released him—no apology, no explanation—he was bruised, dehydrated, and convinced that something fundamental inside him had broken.

Sixteen years later, at fifty-eight, Rajesh held the title of Product Manager at a technology firm in Seattle. His colleagues considered him competent but distant. His wife, Priya, had learned to move carefully around him. He had come to believe, over the years, that people could not be trusted—that beneath every polite interaction lay calculation or potential harm. More than this, he was certain there was something about him that had invited that violence in the first place, some flaw or vulnerability that had marked him as a target. And he was equally certain that nothing good could happen to him anymore; the future held only the possibility of recurrence. These convictions were not abstract. They shaped everything he did.

The belief that he was somehow responsible for what had happened, that he carried an intrinsic fault, drove him to avoid anything that might place him at risk again. He had begun, years ago, to avoid stressors of any kind—not just obvious dangers, but the ordinary friction of daily life. Meetings that might become heated, conversations that veered into personal territory, even social gatherings where he could not predict the flow of interaction. He told himself this was caution. What it meant in practice was isolation. He declined invitations. He left rooms when discussions became animated. At work, he managed this by remaining in his office, communicating mostly through email, delegating tasks that required him to be in shared spaces. Priya had stopped asking him to attend her family dinners.

Yet avoidance fed the very convictions that had spawned it. Each time Rajesh withdrew, each time he constructed another boundary to keep the world at a distance, he reinforced his belief that the world was dangerous and that he could not be part of it. The more he avoided, the more isolated he became, and the more his isolation confirmed his sense that nothing good lay ahead. His constant vigilance about his own body—checking his pulse, monitoring for signs of dizziness or weakness, interpreting a flutter in his chest as a harbinger of collapse—was meant to protect him. Instead, it tethered him to a state of perpetual alarm. He could not relax even when sitting in his own living room, even when Priya sat beside him on the couch. His body remained coiled, ready for the basement, for the voices, for the hands that might appear without warning.

The triggers were everywhere. A siren on the street sent his heart into his throat. Incomprehensible chatter—colleagues speaking rapidly in another language, a podcast playing in the background—immediately transported him back to those three days when meaning had dissolved. A sudden touch from Priya, even her hand on his shoulder in a moment of affection, made him flinch violently, his body interpreting tenderness as threat. He had begun to avoid police officers and security guards, crossing streets to avoid them, his stomach tightening at the sight of a uniform. He had never owned a gun; the thought of weapons made him nauseated. These avoidances made sense to him because they were responses to genuine danger—or so he had come to believe. The fact that he woke most nights to check the locks, to ensure the windows were closed, to verify that Priya was still breathing beside him, felt not like pathology but like necessary vigilance.

It was Priya who finally insisted he seek help. She had found him one night at three in the morning standing in the kitchen, unable to articulate why he had gotten out of bed, only that something felt wrong. She held his face in her hands—carefully, knowing that even this could startle him—and told him she could not watch him disappear any longer. Rajesh sat in the intake appointment carrying the weight of sixteen years, afraid that no one could understand what had been done to him, more afraid still that if he began to speak about it, the world would confirm what he already knew: that he was broken, that he could never be trusted again, and that the best he could hope for was to endure.
